content:
Hello everyone,

I have been learning theorem proving in Lean for some time and I thought it might be time to try to contribute back to mathlib.  After looking at https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/index.html#what-to-contribute-to-mathlib I chose for my first PR an elementary theorem that would probably be a good fit and is not yet in mathlib:

A real function which is continuous on a real interval and whose lower right Dini derivative is nonnegative outside a countable set is monotone.

That is Proposition 2 in Bourbaki, Functions of a Real Variable, Ch. I, §2.2. The Lean proof follows closely Bourbaki's. The PR is #41552

As for my background: my PhD was in differential geometry, and I also became interested in category theory and sheaf theory.  I now work outside academia.

I would appreciate any feedback, on the PR page or on this thread (or any other zulip channel that would be a better fit).

Thanks!
Benoît

Benoît Jubin said:

I would appreciate any feedback

Hey, this is a massive proof. Closely following a paper proof usually does not result in a good Lean proof.
For comparison, Mathlib currently has more than 280,000 theorems, and only 100 of those are longer than 100 lines. While monotoneOn_of_liminf_slope_right_nonneg is almost 200 lines.

Have you considered starting smaller to learn the ropes, such as a PR that adds/changes at most 20 lines?
For example, is there a small lemma you could extract from your proof that you noticed was missing, and would help make your proof shorter?

Thank you for your feedback @Snir Broshi. That statistics is indeed telling. By the way, how can one get such statistics?

The current proof looks indeed too long in retrospect. It is pretty modular, with several intermediate commented goals as haves, so it shouldn't be too hard to extract smaller lemmas. I'll have to think a little bit on their precise API, in order to make them as reusable as possible, so I'm putting the PR as draft in the meantime.

Edit: I began with two small lemmas in #41622
Edit: Another small lemma in #41803

Benoît Jubin said:

By the way, how can one get such statistics?

The total amount of theorems is in Mathlib's stats page.
For the proof length stuff you have to do some manual metaprogramming, and the numbers change depending on what you count exactly, but here's an example in live-lean.
